title: Uposatha
hook: on moon days lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night (AN 8.41)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a clear mind, the fifth precept, the guard at the gate. Your line was keep the mind clear. Did you catch the moment something started to cloud you? Day one hundred twenty-nine.
screen: `A CLEAR MIND — KEEP THE MIND CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Go to a temple in Sri Lanka or Thailand on the night of a full moon and you'll see something unusual. People dressed all in white, lay people, not monks, staying the whole day and into the night. They skip dinner. They leave the jewelry and the perfume at home. Nobody's watching a game on their phone. They're not monks and they aren't trying to become monks. For one day and one night, they're living a little closer to how monks live. It happens every week or so, following the moon. Today's word is that day.
screen: `WHITE CLOTHES, A FULL MOON.` → `NOT MONKS, BUT CLOSE.` → `ONE DAY AND ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Uposatha. It's the observance day, following the phases of the moon: the full moon, the new moon, and in many places the half moons in between. So it comes about once a week. On uposatha days, lay people may take eight precepts instead of five. Precept three becomes complete celibacy for the day. Then three more are added. Not eating after noon. No dancing, singing, music or shows, and no garlands, perfumes or makeup. And no high or luxurious beds: you sleep on something simple. A discourse in the Numerical Discourses lays out these eight, and it has a beautiful way of framing them. For each precept, the lay follower reflects: the arahants, the fully awakened ones, keep this as long as they live. Today, for this one night and day, I'll keep it too, following their example. So it isn't a penance. It's a rehearsal, a day of borrowing a freer life. The word itself is older than Buddhism. It comes from a Sanskrit word for a fast day that Vedic priests kept before a sacrifice. The Vinaya tells that a king, Bimbisara, saw other religious groups gathering on these days and suggested the Buddha's followers gather too. So the monks began meeting on moon days, and to this day they recite their monastic rules together every two weeks. Lay people come to the temple, listen to teaching, sit, and keep their eight precepts. A day kept apart isn't a day taken away from life. It's a day that lets you see the rest of your life more clearly.
screen: `A MOON DAY, ABOUT ONCE A WEEK.` · `EIGHT PRECEPTS FOR A DAY AND NIGHT.` · `FOLLOWING THE ARAHANTS' EXAMPLE.` · `A KING, MOON DAYS, THE MONKS GATHER.` · then, large: `A DAY KEPT APART.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Picture the temple courtyard on a full-moon night: white clothes, a quiet crowd, the moon coming up over the roof. Now picture one day in your own life kept a little apart. What would you set down for it? Maybe the evening snack, the music, the scrolling. You don't have to decide anything now. Just feel what a simpler day might be like. After the bell, look up when the next full moon is. The bell holds the time.
Uposatha. The observance day on the full moon, the new moon and the half moons, when lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night.
Your line: a day kept apart. Today, find out when the next full moon is, and put it in your calendar, with one small thing you'll set down that day. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: On uposatha days many Theravada lay Buddhists go to the temple, often dressed in white, take the eight precepts, listen to teaching and meditate; monks gather every two weeks to recite their monastic rules.

fork.setup: you're keeping eight precepts for the day. it's 3 p.m. and a friend offers you a slice of cake. what does the uposatha day ask?
options: thank them and save it for tomorrow.
fork.reveal: the sixth precept is not eating after noon. many people keep the day by saving the gift for the next morning.

original.note: Pali: the observance day; from Sanskrit upavasatha, a fast day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Buddhist sabbath with strict rules.
what it means: a moon day when lay people borrow a simpler life, keeping eight precepts for a day and a night.
what a scholar hears: upavasatha was the Vedic fast before the soma sacrifice; the Vinaya says Bimbisara asked the Buddha to adopt the day.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.41 (Uposatha Sutta), the eight-factored uposatha
Vinaya, Mahavagga II.1, Bimbisara and the uposatha gathering

notes: The eight precepts and the reflection on following the arahants' example for a night and a day are paraphrased from AN 8.41; confirm.
Bimbisara's suggestion (Vinaya Mahavagga II.1) and the fortnightly patimokkha recitation should be checked.
Etymology from Sanskrit upavasatha (the fast before a Vedic soma sacrifice) is standard but should be confirmed.
Uposatha frequency (full, new and half moons) varies by country and tradition.
